title: How to Listen to Everyone Without Listening to Everyone
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explores a paradox in leadership listening: effective leaders cast a wide net for input from stakeholders and experts, but they don't treat every voice or data point equally. The author describes a 'crap detector' — a critical filter that separates opinion from fact and evidence from unsubstantiated claims — as the tool that lets leaders stay open without becoming overwhelmed or swayed by whoever spoke last. Importantly, leaders conceal which input they value most, which keeps everyone engaged and candid. The piece frames good leaders as detective-like figures who gather broadly but trust their own synthesis over any single source, including high-status ones.
points: Good leaders gather input broadly from many stakeholders but apply what they hear selectively, guided by a reliable internal 'crap detector.'
Leaders deliberately withhold which ideas they value most while gathering input, which keeps every contributor talking openly and feeling included.
Effective listeners distinguish opinions from facts and unsubstantiated claims from evidence rather than accepting input at face value.
Because good leaders stay open to disconfirming information, they're willing to change their view as new evidence arrives, rather than anchoring on early input.
quotes: In other words, they listen to a wide variety of people while selectively deciding what to incorporate into their own thinking.
But without a good “crap detector,” too many opinions can overcomplicate their thinking and slow down their decision-making.
They don’t accept anything at face value. As a matter of course, they distinguish between opinions and facts, and unsubstantiated claims from evidence.
As they generate a viewpoint, they seek information that competes with their newfound perspective, which keeps them talking and listening to those with strong views.

The best leaders are detectives in search of an elusive truth. Like detectives, they listen and learn from everyone, all the while suspecting that much of what they learn is incomplete, biased, and misleading.
